MN202611_1qdwl2qphjk.t:
People exercise in a park in Delhi on Thursday, breathing in hazy, polluted air

There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.

"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.

She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.

Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.

The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.

Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern .

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.

Anti-smog guns sprinkle water to settle atmospheric dust in Delhi

Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.

These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.

Experts say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.

Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

Vehicle entry restrictions have led to huge jams at Delhi's borders

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city . Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.

This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

Why India caps pollution reading at 500 when the air is far more toxic

Can artificial rain fix toxic air in India's capital?

Living in Delhi smog is like watching a dystopian film again and again

In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.

During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".

Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.

A 2025 report , external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.

Burning of crop residue in neighbouring states is among the contributors to Delhi's pollution

For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.

While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.

Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.

Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.

The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others , they are not planning to move out of Delhi.

"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.

"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

MN202611_1i7uddqn9uk.t:
California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in January

California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.

"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.

The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.

The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.

Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.

Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".

California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.

Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in Tennessee

Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".

He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.

Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.

He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".

"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.

"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."

Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.

Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.

He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".

"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.

San Quentin State Prison's used to house California's death row adjustment centre

Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.

At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.

It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.

Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row .

Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.

"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.

Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.

"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.

"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."

Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.

"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.

How widely used is the death penalty in the US?

On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.

While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.

No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.

The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.

California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.

But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

Andy Burnham says it isn't fair if an employer 'holds all the cards'

Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.

The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.

It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning .

Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".

"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.

The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.

He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.

A number of politicians are currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary. , external

Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."

The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union. , external

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna , external , 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

Previous research from the CIPD , external , an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.

But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.

CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".

"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."

Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".

The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".

Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "At a time when employers are finding it harder and harder to take on staff, Labour have decided to make their lives even more difficult.

"It should be up to businesses to decide what information they advertise about job openings, and to decide how to attract the best applicants.

"As long as they are not being dishonest, misleading or discriminatory, it should not be a matter for the government."

Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".

It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.

The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them .

Nottingham Forest's defeat at Brentford was their sixth defeat in 10 games in all competitions this season

Oliver Glasner insists his struggling Nottingham Forest side cannot survive on "flower power" as he tries to find a combination of trust and respect from his squad.

Forest are 19th in the Premier League and winless and goalless at home in the top flight.

Last weekend's 2-0 defeat at Brentford was a fourth defeat in five games as Glasner warned there would be no more compromises after his summer arrival, and he has underlined his standards.

"These are my two values I will never negotiate about, this is trust and respect," he said.

"It can't be one, so if it's just respect, I would say that's military. Then, after a few months of the national service, you are pleased when you can leave."

Glasner drew comparisons with the Woodstock music festival in the 1960s.

"When it's just trust, it's a flower power, just flying," he said. "Everybody can do what he wants and it's nice and great - Woodstock - but it's not high-performance Woodstock.

"Military is [high performance], to be honest, because otherwise this huge organisation couldn't work, and I felt we had too much Woodstock.

"We need a good balance between Woodstock, having fun, but also military, high performance. That's the most important thing, high performance, because that's what we get paid for, that's our job. If we have this - fly."

When asked by BBC Sport if he should have told his players sooner Glasner said: "I always ask myself this question - should I have done it earlier?

"Of course, maybe two or three times I felt it's time and then I thought 'no, come on Oliver, be patient and maybe things change'.

"Then it seemed to be the same game [ Brentford ] like the last ones, so I felt I have to say it now because otherwise things won't change."

Glasner is not under immediate pressure and remains in close communication with the Forest hierarchy, with stability desired after four managers last season.

The 52-year-old has made a positive impression with his work and methods, even if there have been some obvious grumbles from players who are not playing, and there remains a desire to stay calm.

"I'm always in contact with the ownership," Glasner said. "It's not always Mr [Evangelos] Marinakis because he has other stuff to do, but there is his son [Miltiadis], George [Syrianos, chief football officer] and Pedro [Ferreira, technical director] here at the training ground, and Theodore [Giannikos] the CEO.

"There's always communication - and that's a good thing, because everybody understands better why I am how I am. I never say what's best for Oliver Glasner, because I don't feel important. I will always say what I believe is best for Nottingham Forest , for the club.

"I don't like to accept things if I feel they are wrong. My addiction is to succeed with Nottingham Forest and, right now, I have failed. Then I get really upset with myself because I want to meet the expectations of the players, owner and the fans.

"Right now, I've failed and that's why I blame myself most."

BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert FPL Heisenberg gives his answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers heading into gameweek 10.

Despite performing so well in recent weeks - helping Arsenal to three clean sheets in three Premier League games - for me defender Ezri Konsa (£4.8m) is not a buy this week.

After the midweek Champions League game, Mikel Arteta mentioned him having some knee problems, which led to his early substitution.

William Saliba is now fit and was even in the squad, so anyone bringing Konsa in now is looking at a sell as early as gameweek 11.

However, for owners he is not an automatic sell either.

There is still a chance he starts Hull at home. I am hoping he either starts or he isn't in the squad.

As an owner I am hoping he is fit enough to start, and then in gameweek 11 or 12 I will look to move him on to a defender with strong defensive-contribution potential - someone like Brighton 's Luka Vuskovic (£5.2m), Liverpool 's Jeremy Jacquet (£5.1m) or Leeds ' Tarik Muharemovic (£5.1m).

We are in a period of the game where defenders look very strong - they offer goal threat, defensive contributions and play for sides with real defensive strength. The days of starting five midfielders feel in the past for now. The meta is closer to four defenders, three or four midfielders, and two or three strikers. Things can shift quickly in FPL, but that is the landscape right now.

If you have midfielders you are not happy with, the answer may not always be to sell them. It can be to bench them some weeks and only play them in the better fixtures.

In isolation, Nottingham Forest 's Morgan Gibbs-White (£7.8m) is still a reasonable pick. He is on penalties, he is the talisman for Forest even when the goals have been scarce, and he plays 90 minutes.

Bryan Mbeumo (£7.9m) is involved in a lot of chances and goals for a Manchester United side that is struggling. He was unlucky not to return against Chelsea .

Kevin Schade (£6.2m) plays for a Brentford team that is on the up and carries attacking threat.

These are decent options. You do not have to force a sale just because they have blanked recently.

There is no clear must-buy in midfield, unless you are without Brighton 's Pascal Gross (£6.2m) or Chelsea 's Morgan Rogers (£8.2m) and you specifically need to move one of these three on. Hold if you can, and reassess if the picture changes.

We are entering a busier stretch where some of the early-season reliable options - Konsa (£4.8m), Brighton 's Maxim de Cuyper (£5.4m) and Arsenal 's Riccardo Calafiori (£5.9m) - may not be as nailed as they have been.

I am not saying sell them all immediately, but it is worth starting to think about how you phase in the next wave of defensive purchases.

Antonio Silva (£5.1m) or James Hill (£5.6m) at Bournemouth both stand out as good options this week and beyond. The underlying defensive data has been solid, and both are excellent for defensive contributions - more than nine per 90 minutes. Playing Ipswich is a decent time to buy.

Muharemovic at Leeds is another. Spurs is not the easiest fixture, but Leeds have been very good at Elland Road, so it is a fair entry point if you want him.

A Liverpool defender is also worth considering. Crystal Palace have struggled and have been vulnerable to set-pieces - Tottenham 's Jan Paul van Hecke had a number of chances and eventually scored last week. Virgil van Dijk (£6.4m) or Jacquet look shrewd buys. If you do not already own De Cuyper, or if you can afford Gabriel (£8.0m), those remain strong options too.

This is the start of a good run, beginning with Crystal Palace . There are a few options, but each carries some risk. The defenders are the obvious options - Jacquet and Van Dijk both look fine. Midfield is harder.

Bradley Barcola (£8.1m) is getting minutes but the underlying numbers have not been strong. Cody Gakpo (£7.1m) has shown good minutes and data in the past, but the recent early substitutions are a concern while he is competing with Victor Munoz (£6.5m) and Barcola out wide.

Dominik Szoboszlai (£6.7m) has been underwhelming. He is not getting enough game time and his role is unclear. That leaves Alexander Isak (£9.2m).

He is an excellent pick, but at more than £9m he is also expensive. You have to ask why you would take him over Nicolas Jackson (£7.0m), Joao Pedro (£7.7m) and Erling Haaland (£15.8m), or the cheaper options like Thierno Barry (£5.6m) and Dominic Calvert-Lewin (£6.1m). He is good, but he also blocks other good picks. It is perfectly reasonable to wait and look again around gameweek 13, rather than forcing investment now.

Haaland is away at Nottingham Forest . Forest have struggled at both ends, but their attacking and defensive data has actually been reasonable, and Glasner has a history of being difficult to break down against stronger sides from his Palace days. If you want to take on Haaland, this is a reasonable week to do it.

The problem is the alternative options are limited.

The clearest ones are Gabriel or Calafiori. Gabriel brings excellent clean-sheet odds, the chance of a bullet header, and defensive-contribution points. He is probably the strongest rival to Haaland.

In my own team I am looking at Calafiori. He had a full midweek rest so he should start against Hull , and when Arsenal dominate the ball he gets very high up the pitch. Against Hull that could be significant.

We have to start treating defenders as genuine captaincy options given how many double-digit hauls they have produced this season.

My head is still on the safer Haaland pick, but I am very tempted by Calafiori. If you want to go different, an Arsenal defender is the way to go.

This is Atiku Abubakar's seventh attempt to become Nigeria's president

Nigeria's Federal High Court has sacked the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) party - and also ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid.

A statement from the ADC said the ruling was another desperate attempt to cripple the opposition.

Presidential elections are scheduled to take place on 16 January when President Bola Tinubu's main challengers are again expected to be Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.

Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.

As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.

But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.

Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.

This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.

In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.

Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"

In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.

The ADC says it will challenge the ruling at the Court of Appeal.

In a statement on Facebook, Abubakar, 79, said he would contest the election despite the ruling , external .

"Let me be clear to every Nigerian who has stood with us: I am in this race. I am not going anywhere. We will be on the ballot. No threat, blackmail or court manoeuvre will make me abandon you or the cause we share," he wrote on Friday.

He had previously questioned the timing of the judgment, coming "barely a day after a mammoth crowd turned out in Sokoto [northern Nigeria] to welcome him" as he launched his campaign.

Political parties in Nigeria have increasingly been taking internal issues to court.

But as it stands, the electoral commission has issued its final list of candidates , external - and Abubakar is on the ticket for the ADC with former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi as his running mate.

The ADC is seen as the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.

The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.

Peter Obi - the other main presidential candidate, who is on the ballot for a second time - said he was shocked by Thursday's high court ruling.

He released a statement on X with the heading , external : "Do not undermine democracy".

The 65-year-old went on to say: "My concern is that three months before a general election, it is in the public interest to have certainty.

Obi had briefly joined the ADC before leaving earlier this year to join the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) - in part because of the legal challenges within the ADC.

"The sustenance of democracy in Nigeria, in the midst of encroaching military rule in West Africa, should strengthen our resolve to protect opposition politics and not stamp out opposition parties," he said.

The NDC's candidate said that, as president, he would ensure that the existence of opposition parties would be respected.

"This is a time to strengthen our democracy by allowing the opposition to thrive."

Inteko ishinga amategeko yatoye Umushinga w’Itegeko ryerekeye Inshingano (Draft Law on Obligations).Ni itegeko rije gukemura ibibazo bishingiye ku masezerano, n’amakosa akorwa hagati y’abantu, ariko bikaba bitakemurwaga neza n'amategeko asanzwe.

Ni itegeko rigena ibyerekeye inshingano zikomoka ku masezerano, harimo n’ubwumvikane hagati y'impande zombi (nk'amasezerano y'ubukode, aho zimwe mu ngingo zaryo ziteganya uburyo amafaranga y'ubukode ashobora kongerwa cyangwa kugabanywa).

Iryo tegeko kandi rigena ibijyanye n’inshingano zikomoka ku bisa n’amasezerano (Quasi-contracts), urugero nk’igihe urukiko rutegetse umuntu kwishyura undi bitaturutse ku masezerano bari bafitanye mbere. Rivuga kandi ku nshingano zikomoka ku makosa no ku bisa n’amakosa (Torts/Delicts), harimo ingaruka z'ibikorwa umuntu akora bikagira ingaruka ku bandi, byaba byagenderewe cyangwa bitagenderewe.

Mu gihe cyo gutora ingingo ku yindi mu zigize uwo mushinga w’itegeko mbere y’uko ritorwa muri rusange, abadepite bagiye babaza ibibazo ku ngingo zimwe na zimwe babona ko zidasobanutse neza cyangwa se ko zirimo icyuho mu bisobanuro byazo, maze umuyobozi wa Komisiyo ibishinzwe agatanga ibisobanuro.

Depite Mukandekezi Francoise ni umwe mu babajije ikibazo ku ngingo ya 642 ivuga ku bijyanye n’ubwikorezi, aho iyo ngingo ivuga ku ibura ry’ugomba kwakira ibintu, kwanga kubyakira cyangwa se kugira uburangare mu kubyakira.

Yagize ati,” …Agaka ka kabiri karavuga ngo icyakora,iyo hari impamvu yihutirwa, umwikorezi,ashobora kwikuraho ibintu byangirika,atabanje kubimenyesha, uwabimuhaye. Ndibaza impamvu yihutirwa, yatuma umwikorezi yikuraho ibintu bamuhaye gutwara atamenyesheje uwabimuhaye yaba ari iyihe? Ikindi ibintu byangirika biri mu bwoko bwinshi, ashobora kuba ari amata, ashobora kuba ari inyama, bishobora kuba amafi n’ibindi, ese aramutse bamuhaye gutwara ibintu agasanga ubyakira adahari cyangwa se adashaka kubyakira, guhita ahabwa uburenganzibra bwo kuba yabyikuraho, ntibyatanga icyuho cyo kunyereza umutungo? Numva iyi ngingo yatanga icyuho, utwara ibintu akaba yabinyereza kubera ko ubyakira atamubonye”.

Asubiza icyo kibazo, Perezida wa Komisiyo y’Imiyoborere, Uburinganire n’Ubwuzuzanye bw’Abagabo n’Abagore, Nabahire Anastase, yavuze ko iyo ngingo ivuga byinshi umwikorezi yahura nabyo n’uko yabyitwaramo.

Yagize ati,” …iyo ugomba kwakira ibintu atabonetse, yanze kubyakira cyangwa se agize uburangare mu kubyakira,cyangwa iyo umwikorezi nta kosa afite, adashobora kubera impamvu iyo ari yo yose gushyikiriza ibyo yikoreye ugomba kubyakira, ahita abimenyesha uwabyohereje, kandi akamusaba kumumenyesha uko bagomba kugenza ibyo bintu. Aka gaka ubwako karatwereka ibintu byinshi cyane byaba ku mwikorezi uvuye Mombasa,yagera i Kigali aho agomba gushyitsa ibintu, akabura uwo agomba kubishyitsaho, yabimugezaho se akabyanga, yashaka se telefoni ye akayibura, agahabwa inshingano yo guhita amenyesha uwamutumye uri Mombasa ibimubayeho, niba hari undi bakorana yabigezaho, cyangwa niba yabigarura, cyangwa niba hari aho yabigurisha,…”.

“ Igika cya Kabiri kiravuga ngo icyakora iyo hari impamvu zihutirwa, umwikorezi, ashobora kwikuraho ibintu byangirika yagejeje aho agomba kubigeza atabanje kumenyesha uwabimuhaye…”.

Depite Nabahire Anastase yifashishije urugero rw’umucunda (uvana amata ku kiraro cy’inka ayajyana ku ikusanyirizo), yavuze ko uwo mucunda ashobora kugemura amata yagera aho ku ikusanyirizo agasanga hafunze. Kandi amata yangirika vuba, yareba akabona ko litiro 50 cyangwa 100 zigiye gupfa, yagerageza kumenyesha uwamutumye, agasanga telefoni itariho, aho ngo haba hari impamvu zihutirwa, aho kugira ngo ayo mata amwangirikane ngo ashobora kuyagemura ahandi, nyuma akabisobanura. Impamvu, ni uko utwara ibintu aba afite inshingano zo kubyitaho nubwo atari ibye, ariko igihe abifite mu ntoki aba agomba kubyitaho kugira ngo arinde inyungu z’uwo akorera.

A large convoy of emergency vehicles transported the man to the Royal Free Hospital in north London

A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been flown back to the UK.

The man, who has not been identified, landed at RAF Northolt before being transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.

Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of the All Hazards Public Health Response team at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said there are "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and the risk to the public remains low.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

The infected doctor was brought to the UK on a medical evacuation flight as part of a joint effort by the UK and DR Congo governments and their international health partners, the Department of Health (DoH) said.

A convoy of emergency vehicles were on hand to complete the transfer following the man's arrival at the RAF base.

Three large police vans travelled at either end of the convoy, while two ambulances and another support car were involved.

Traffic was stopped and police exited the vans to keep the public away as the convoy arrived at the Royal Free Hospital.

The man is now being treated in a "highly specialised" isolation unit at the hospital, the DoH said.

The Royal Free Hospital successfully treated three health workers who had been evacuated after the Ebola outbreak in West Africa in 2014 and 2015.

There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

None of these cases have resulted in a death.

The plane carrying the infected man arrived at RAF Northolt on Thursday

There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa in the 2010s.

The current outbreak in DR Congo has a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.

Ebola can result in serious illness and death. Early symptoms include vomiting and diarrhoea but it can progress to organ failure and internal bleeding.

The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The ongoing outbreak centred on DR Congo is fuelled by the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.

There is no approved vaccine but the World Health Organization said experts have recommended adding two new candidate drugs to an ongoing clinical trial.

The vaccines, one developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and another by the firm Moderna, will join the trial once they are approved by Congolese health authorities.

It will be the first time jabs specifically designed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus are tested during an outbreak.

Since the outbreak, Ebola cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

MN202611_1phwxfbp45x.t: African countries face significant legal hurdles in seeking reparations for slavery and colonialism, including the difficulty of proving that these practices violated international law when they occurred. A shortage of African international lawyers to help governments pursue such claims presents another challenge, a leading legal expert has warned. ALSO READ: Rwanda to host major conference on colonial reparations Moïse Makane Mbengue, President of the African Society of International Law (AfSIL) who is currently in Kigali, said African governments were increasingly aware of the need to use international law to advance their interests, but that awareness alone was not enough without the expertise to navigate its complexities. “Sometimes states are not reluctant to use international law. Sometimes the problem is the knowledge of international law,” he told The New Times in an interview ahead of AfSIL’s 15th Annual Conference, which opens in Kigali on Thursday, November 5, and runs until November 7. Mbengue, a professor of international law at the University of Geneva in Switzerland and an affiliated professor at Sciences Po Paris in France, said the continent needed to strengthen its legal capacity to turn longstanding demands for reparations into claims that can be pursued through international mechanisms. ALSO READ: How colonialism disconnected Rwandans from ancestral identity Legal barriers to historical claims One of the main obstacles, he explained, lies in the law of state responsibility, which requires a country seeking reparations to prove that the conduct of the state it is claiming against was contrary to international law at the time it happened. This complicates claims arising from slavery and colonisation because international law did not prohibit those practices in the way it does today. “Slavery, when it happened in the 16th, 17th, 18th century, international law at that time was not prohibiting slavery. So those European nations that engaged into acts of slavery, they were not, properly speaking, violating international law at that time,” he said. “The same for colonisation. At the time when colonisation happened, international law was not prohibiting nations, some nations to colonise as a people.” He acknowledged this as one of the major limitations African countries face when seeking to establish the responsibility of former colonial powers. Despite the legal hurdles, Mbengue said there were reasons to remain optimistic, particularly as international law continues to evolve and the international community increasingly recognises the consequences of historical injustices. He cited a United Nations General Assembly resolution adopted last year on slavery as a crime, saying it had helped move the reparations debate beyond political demands towards the legal means of pursuing claims. “Most of the rhetoric, most of the narrative surrounding reparations since independence was very political, very political, very maybe even philosophical. But last year was a turning point,” he said. “There has been a shift in the narrative. There has been a shift in the conversation from a more political conversation to now a more legal conversation.” He added that recognition of the harm caused by colonisation and growing calls for the return of cultural property looted from Africa had opened pathways that countries could pursue. ALSO READ: Rwanda’s independence served colonial interests, say experts Africa needs more international law expertss Mbengue said the ability to take advantage of these developments also depends on having enough African lawyers with the expertise to advise governments and represent them in international proceedings. He pointed to Rwanda’s case against the United Kingdom before the Permanent Court of Arbitration and Mauritius’ efforts to seek an advisory opinion on its decolonisation process as examples of African countries increasingly using international law to advance their claims. Rwanda, he said, had made progress by involving more African lawyers and arbitrators in its international litigation. He urged other governments to invest in training a new generation of experts. “If you want international law to serve African interests, you need to think more about having African international lawyers presenting the claims of our states,” he said. He said he was not opposed to involving lawyers from outside the continent, noting that diverse teams could bring valuable experience. However, he argued that African lawyers should have a stronger presence in cases involving African countries. “For our needs to be better reflected, for our needs to be better taken into account in the interpretation and application of international law, you need to work with those who understand the needs of African countries, with those who understand the challenges of African countries,” he said. He described this as part of the effort towards the “Africanisation of international law”, which seeks to ensure that African voices influence the making, interpretation and application of international legal rules. Reparations extend beyond compensation The Kigali conference will examine the legal tools and procedures available to African states seeking reparations for slavery, colonisation and the looting of cultural property. Mbengue stressed that reparations should not be understood only as financial compensation. They can also involve restitution, including the return of cultural objects and ancestral property taken from the continent. “Reparations can also be about restitution, return of our property, return of our cultural property, of our ancestral property,” he said. The discussions will also examine the challenges of establishing claims and calculating compensation, as well as the future implications of climate change. Mbengue said African countries should begin developing a legal position on loss and damage arising from climate change, noting that the continent has historically contributed only about 3 to 4 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions but is expected to be among the regions most affected by its impacts. “We need to build already today a narrative, an African vision, an African strategy for loss and damages deriving from climate change impacts,” he said. “We need to fight already for the future.” He said the reparations debate should also involve Caribbean and Latin American countries, which share histories of slavery, colonisation and cultural property looting with African nations. “Unity is power,” he said, adding that the issue had become a broader Global South concern, although Africa needed to ensure its own experiences and perspectives were represented. AfSIL, which Mbengue has led since 2017, was established in 2012 in Brazzaville, Republic of Congo. It brings together international lawyers from Africa and other parts of the world and seeks to spread knowledge of international law across the continent while supporting governments in strengthening their legal capacity. The annual conferences address issues affecting African countries. Previous meetings have examined peaceful settlement of disputes, climate change, foreign investment, natural resources and the law of the sea. Mbengue said the organisation publishes the proceedings of its conferences so that governments, practitioners, researchers and future generations can use the discussions as a reference. It also plans to follow the Kigali meeting with seminars, capacity-building sessions and technical support to governments. “Without knowing the law, you cannot use the law. Without knowing the law, you cannot know the limits of the law, but how to then circumvent those limits or transcend those limits,” he said.

MN202611_gxlnywekfq.t:
Waste dumped at the landfill site on the outskirts of Finningley

More than 1,000 tonnes of "sewage sludge" have been seen at a landfill site near Doncaster, according to an MP for the town.

Lee Pitcher said in a Facebook post he had been told the waste was being stored in "an uncovered stockpile" at the site in Finningley.

The Labour MP said he had been in contact with the Environment Agency (EA), which confirmed on Thursday that it had "set out a series of actions" for the site's operator following an inspection.

The landfill, located in a former quarry, is operated by Tetron Finningley Ltd, which has not previously responded when contacted for comment by the BBC.

Pitcher, who is the MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, said EA officers visited the landfill on 9 October and, after he "chased" them for their findings, they responded on Tuesday.

He said the EA had told him that during the visit "approximately 1,000 tonnes of sewage sludge were observed being stored externally in an uncovered stockpile" and had "identified concerns regarding whether site activities were being undertaken in accordance with the operating techniques and management arrangements described within the approved documents".

Pitcher said the EA had given the landfill operator until 10 November to resolve the issue.

The MP said he had subsequently contacted the EA again about "potential asbestos disposal at the site, along with the air quality and environmental ramifications this could bring".

A nearby motocross track closed after riders complained of headaches and dizziness they blamed on the smell coming from the site

Last month, Ed Bradley, a director of the neighbouring Doncaster Moto Parc, said he had been forced to close the venue after people attending the motocross track were suffering from "headaches, nausea and generally feeling unwell" from the smells .

He said he was concerned that the business may no longer be viable if it continues to remain closed.

In a statement on Facebook, he said: "For months, we have raised concerns about the terrible odours coming from the neighbouring site, the effects on our staff and customers, and our inability to operate safely.

"Despite those reports, the situation has continued.

"Unfortunately, while the authorities have been investigating, the financial consequences for Doncaster Moto Parc have been devastating.

"We are now facing the very real possibility of losing the business altogether."

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "We expect site operators to manage odour effectively and have identified issues around odour management at this site.

"Following an inspection, we have set out a series of actions that we expect the operator to comply with and will not hesitate to take further enforcement action should that be required."

MN202611_qg7tm10q2v.t:
Authorities will be scrambling to follow any information that might lead them to a culprit

The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another.

At least 21 flights and several airports across Europe were affected by bomb threats on Thursday .

In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it.

They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not be real.

It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia.

Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.

There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.

Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence.

Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?

But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them.

There was the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State".

That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021.

Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.

But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.

For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

Depth: relative distance from the camera.

Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

See the data contract and action schema .

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.

Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.

Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.

Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

Transfer-auto : Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.

Sim-auto : Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.

Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.

Sim-Bimanual : Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

MN202611_84htflapwf.t:
The shootings took place in rural areas northeast of the city of Afyonkarahisar (pictured)

Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.

The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.

The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in Eskişehir province.

CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.

Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.

Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.

Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.

The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.

In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".

Uyu mukobwa utwite inda y’imvutsi, avuga ko uyu yitaga umugabo we, yafashwe ubwo we yajyaga kwisuzumisha mu Kigo Nderabuzima giherereye mu Murenge wa Mugina, abaforomokazi bamusaba ko ahamagara uwo musore wamuteye inda.

Umusore ahageze yasanze bateguye Umugenzacyaha wa Isange One stop Center, bamwambika amapingu guhera uwo munsi ahita afungwa.

Ati: “Nageze mu cyumba cy’iburanisha ntungurwa no kumva Umushinjacyaha asabiye uyu musore igifungo cy’imyaka 25.”

Yavuze ko yahise asohoka muri icyo cyumba avuza induru, yigaragura ku isima yibaza aho azakura ubufasha, kubera ko amafaranga yo kwishyura Ibitaro n’imyenda y’uruhinja ateganya kubyara azabihabwa n’uyu musore.

Uyu mukobwa utazi icyo amategeko y’u Rwanda avuga, yabwiye Umunyamakuru ko yakuze mu buzima bugoranye kubera ko ababyeyi be bamaze igihe baratandukanye ku buryo nyina afite uburwayi bwo mu mutwe, naho Se akaba atazi aho aherereye.

Avuga ko bari bamaranye igihe kinini we n’uyu musore babana nk’umugabo n’umugore.

Gitifu w’Umurenge wa Mugina Munyakazi Epimaque avuga ko nta makuru y’umukobwa n’umusore babanaga yari afite, akavuga ko ibyo bakoze bigize icyaha, ariko ko bagiye gushakira ubufasha uyu mukobwa wakorewe ihohoterwa bakamufasha kubona icumbi, ndetse n’ibigomba kumutunga.

Ati: “Mumubwire aze aturebe, kandi ikibazo cye twiteguye kugikemura.”

Iyo umuntu mukuru asambanyije umwana bigakurikirwa no kumugira umugabo cyangwa umugore, igihano kiba igifungo cya burundu. Ingingo ya 133 y’Itegeko nº 68/2018 ryo ku wa 30/08/2018 riteganya ibyaha n’ibihano muri rusange ihinduwe ku buryo bukurikira: Umuntu ukorera ku mwana kimwe mu bikorwa bishingiye ku gitsina bikurikira, aba akoze icyaha: gushyira igitsina cy’umuntu mu gitsina, mu kibuno cyangwa mu kanwa by’umwana; umuntu uhamijwe n’urukiko gukora kimwe mu bikorwa bivugwa mu gika cya (11) cy’iyi ngingo ahanishwa igifungo kitari munsi y’imyaka 20 ariko kitarenze imyaka 25.

Nkeka ko bali bakwiye kureka uyu musore bakibanira.Nubundi abenshi babana barabanje kuryamana.Abafunga abantu kimwe n’abacamanza,abenshi nabo barasambana.Ni icyaha gikorwa ku bwinshi kurusha ibindi byaha byose.Iteka gusambana bigira ingaruka,nubwo bikundwa na benshi. Nubwo abantu miliyoni na miliyoni baryamana n’abo batashakanye mu rwego rwo kwishimisha,Ijambo ry’Imana rivuga ko abasambanyi,kimwe n’abandi bose bakora ibyo Imana itubuza,batazaba mu bwami bw’imana.Ntacyo bimaze kwishimisha akanya gato,hanyuma bikazakubuza ubuzima bw’iteka muli Paradizo kandi ntuzazuke ku Munsi w’Imperuka wegereje.Ni ukutagira ubwenge nyakuli (lack of wisdom).

MN202611_i75xliyu2c.t:
Watch: US First Lady Melania Trump given Ukraine's highest award for women

US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.

The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

The Kremlin envoy also met Donald Trump, the US president later revealed to reporters.

Trump refused to say what they had discussed, but confirmed he had not met the Ukrainian delegation. "There's going to be an agreement," he asserted, "it's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... and I could even say it might involve all of Europe."

Melania Trump handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia "personal letters" for their respective presidents

Melania Trump was credited by both delegations at the White House with playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.

The US first lady said she had "reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources" during the truce.

"Last week in Oleshky and neighbouring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022," Trump said. "They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions."

She thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when the Russian president launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.

Dmitriev, a businessman and special Putin envoy who has previously represented Moscow during peace talks with Ukraine, thanked the US first lady for "saving and touching so many lives".

"Let us continue making a humanitarian contribution together; this is within our power," Dmitriev said, before gifting Melania Trump a framed drawing by an 11-year-old Oleshky evacuee.

He also praised Trump for her work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. These include children allegedly abducted by Russia.

Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament who has also been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team, said the Oleshky ceasefire had constituted the "biggest de-escalation since 2022".

"We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning the… mechanics of how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes," he added.

He acknowledged that the "political track" of negotiations to end the conflict was "complex" but said Ukrainians were asking Melania Trump "to keep going and find new missions and de-escalate more."

At the end of the event, Trump handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia two letters to be hand-delivered to their respective presidents.

The White House later said Melania Trump had invited her guests to view two historic artifacts which she had "personally selected as powerful symbols of peace".

One was an 18th Century medicine chest which was removed from the White House when the British set it on fire in 1812. "Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance," the White House said.

The second artifact was a cup gifted in 1899 to the French ambassador in recognition of his efforts to bring the Spanish-American war to an end.

Melania Trump has generally remained discreet on foreign policy matters, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv have elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement in coordinating the delicate ceasefire - the most enduring and widespread of the war so far.

A source who works in the local government of the Kherson region told the BBC that work on the Oleshky evacuation had been ongoing for almost a year.

Oleshky evacuees arrived in Ukraine after a journey through southern Russia and Belarus

However, the source said, "at a certain point other individuals became involved, seemingly after most of the groundwork had already been laid and subsequently began taking credit for the progress that had been made."

It was difficult to determine exactly who had played what role and at which stage of the process, the source acknowledged, adding that "those who had been directly involved in the negotiations for nearly a year were eventually prohibited from communicating publicly about the matter."

Speaking after the meeting in the White House had taken place, President Zelensky said the success of the Oleshky ceasefire "had proved a very simple thing: when Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops."

"The same applies to our people who are held in Russian captivity. When Putin wants, they go home."

A source close to American officials shared a similar assessment, implying to the BBC that despite the outward praise, "the person who made [the ceasefire] possible, whether we like it or not, is essentially Putin."

"And this was done in order to pass the ball to [Donald] Trump... so that it would have some positive effect for his midterm elections."

There has been no change whatsoever in Russia's position, Ukrainian political analyst Dmytro Levus told the BBC.

Moscow "agreed to it because there was pressure from the American side... In doing so, the Russians confirmed Zelenskyy's words that, when necessary, it turns out Russia can quickly stop firing and even maintain that ceasefire."

As the frontline region of Kherson experienced its first six days of peace in several years, the rest of Ukraine continued to come under Russian attack.

This week, several drone and missile attacks killed and injured civilians across the country. On Monday alone, more than 40 people were killed in a single Russian strike on an aid distribution centre in the region of Zaporizhzhia. More are thought to still be buried under the rubble.

Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv

MN202611_yi9syz1qdl.t:
Thomas Tuchel will name his next England squad on Friday

England have made medical checks on Cole Palmer as Thomas Tuchel considers whether to select the Chelsea forward in his next squad.

The 24-year-old missed all four games during the previous international window with a minor injury.

He completed 90 minutes for Chelsea against Brentford before those matches, and started for the Blues in the first game afterwards.

Tuchel, who names his squad to face Croatia and Spain on Friday, said at the time that Palmer was "playing with discomfort and pain" but was "missing too many opportunities" with England.

Whether he is recalled will be a key theme on Friday. While it is normal for England medical staff to check on players under consideration, it also underlines that Palmer remains on Tuchel's radar despite his stark comments in September.

In addition to deciding whether to select Palmer, head coach Tuchel has a number of other dilemmas to resolve.

Bukayo Saka's injury absence opens the door to another attacker, with his Arsenal team-mate Noni Madueke pushing for a recall following a string of impressive performances.

Manchester United forward Marcus Rashford has not played since mid-October and is not fit for selection, while Chelsea defender Trevoh Chalobah is a major injury doubt.

Defenders Ben White and Djed Spence are pushing for recalls after missing out on the previous squad through injury.

The likes of Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Declan Rice and many others are now stonewall selections - but the intrigue is around the remaining few spots still seemingly up for grabs.

Will some old faces earn a recall or will there be new faces soon pulling on the England shirt? BBC Sport runs down some of the potential candidates for selection.

The 19-year-old Fulham midfielder has already been close to a senior England debut.

King travelled to the US as part of the preparation squad before the World Cup, along with Alex Scott, Ethan Nwaneri and Rio Ngumoha.

Scott and Ngumoha have already made their debuts for the senior side and Nwaneri is currently on loan at Borussia Dortmund.

Tuchel said in his last news conference how King is close to a senior call-up and the midfielder has impressed for England Under-21s too.

The biggest challenge for King will be finding a chance to shine in his favoured number 10 position with Bellingham being England's best midfielder and the position being one of real strength for the Three Lions.

Will Lankshear has been prolific for Middlesbrough this season

There is a lack of number nines in the English game and the job of being Harry Kane's understudy is harder than it sounds.

The England captain has just won the Ballon d'Or, likes to play almost every minute for his country and is the captain, record goalscorer and arguably the best player in Tuchel's side.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has been selected in the squads before and since the World Cup but, despite doing well for Leeds, it has not quite clicked for him under Tuchel and he was given just 15 minutes in two substitute appearances in the last window.

Tuchel has started to use Bellingham as the back-up to Kane, but he could opt for more of a prospect in his squad in this shorter window and turn to Lankshear.

The 21-year-old striker, who like Kane started at Tottenham, was sold to Middlesbrough this summer for £20m and has scored 15 goals in all competitions so far this campaign.

He has scored 13 goals in as many games in the Championship, helping Middlesbrough to the top of the division.

He only made his debut for the England Under-21s during the last international window and scored in that game so it would be quite a rise for a player who is not in the Premier League.

Tuchel is aware of Lankshear and with a lack of number nines across the age groups it could be an interesting option for a manager who is not afraid of making big calls.

He did miss Middlesbrough's loss to Wrexham on Wednesday with a tweaked hamstring but could return in time for Saturday.

The Everton number 10 has turned down call-ups from the Republic of Ireland as he focuses on his dream of trying to represent the Three Lions.

He has been one of the Toffees' standout performers having scored two goals and registered two assists in all competitions, helping Everton to seventh in the league.

Dewsbury-Hall, 28, is a clever technician with an eye for a pass and his ability on the ball would likely suit international football.

But team-mate James Garner, who Tuchel called a mini-Valverde, was called up before Dewsbury-Hall when there were dropouts in the last international break with that showing perhaps he has more to do to get on Tuchel's radar.

Gibbs-White was probably the unluckiest player to be left out of the initial squad last time around when Tuchel got his players together in September.

But the Nottingham Forest midfielder was called up as a late replacement after a number of high profile pull-outs and left a family holiday to join up with the Three Lions squad.

Tuchel values that kind of dedication and referenced the willingness of Gibbs-White, 26, to join up.

The Forest captain featured during every game of the last break although he did not start a game.

But with Forest struggling at the bottom end of the Premier League table - and competing against the likes of Bellingham, Phil Foden, Palmer and Eberechi Eze - the midfielder could miss out again.

A must pick or unreliable? Tuchel's Palmer dilemma

White has been unlucky since he ended his international hiatus to return in March.

The Arsenal defender missed the World Cup with a knee injury that forced him to also miss the Champions League final.

White then missed the first England squad of this campaign with injury, with Tuchel saying the 29-year-old would have been called up if he had been fit, citing his partnership with Saka as potentially good for the Three Lions.

But White has been available for all but one of Arsenal's games this season and would add a quality defensive option at right-back if selected, especially with Reece James missing through injury.

Henderson has not been in the England set-up since the World Cup, where he fell over an advertising hoarding following the win over Mexico in the Azteca Stadium and broke his arm.

Many would have thought the 36-year-old's international career was over but Henderson, then at Brentford, made a move to Chelsea as they looked to add experience to their young squad.

After recovering from the arm injury, Henderson has surprised some to become an important part of the Chelsea midfield, starting five games in a row and scoring twice in a win over Bournemouth, before he missed the Blues' win over Manchester United with injury.

Henderson is a popular figure, respected by staff and players and is again performing at the top level.
