MN202611_d01srbup85.t:
The visit of Tarantino and Minogue to Porthcawl has become the stuff of legends in the local pub and community

Sharing a pint with Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction director Quentin Tarantino in his local pub was a surreal experience for a Welsh filmmaker.

But this was just the tip of the iceberg for Jamie Adams, who also managed to get singing icon Kylie Minogue and rapper RZA from the Wu-Tang Clan to Porthcawl for his new movie.

The arrival of the stars in the seaside town earlier this year to work on Tangled Up in Blue caused a buzz, and Adams admitted it felt like "an out of body experience" bringing his heroes to his hometown.

It is not the first time he has brought big names to south Wales, having worked with Dirty Dancing star Jennifer Grey on 2019 film Bittersweet Symphony.

Adams was able to include scenes in locations that mean a lot to him, including the pub his dad used to run.

"It was called the Ship and Castle then and the bar is actually a boat that he brought from Weymouth, which is where I was born," he said.

"So I've got Quentin Tarantino having a pint with me in my dad's old pub, talking to Neil, one of my old pals, who I've known since I was like eight years old.

Tangled Up in Blue follows a talent manager (Tarantino) who has spent 40 years managing legends but finds himself stranded at a hotel bar caught between an old flame and a lost soul.

It all fell into place with the involvement of the superstars after Adams filmed in France in 2025.

Adams (second from left) uses techniques in his films that mean they are filmed quickly with improvisation

He shot a movie there in a week in his usual improv style - which is where much of it is created spontaneously rather than being read from a pre-written script.

Adams said Tarantino thoroughly enjoyed it, and described it as reminding him of French New Wave cinema that emerged from the late 1950s to the late 1960s.

"I said [to him] I'd love to do one that was a little bit more personal to me and actually shot in in my hometown," Adams added.

Getting Minogue, who has described herself as "half Welsh" to be part of the project was even easier.

Her family actually hail from near Porthcawl, with mum Carol Jones and her Welsh-speaking Nain , external Millie Jones emigrating from Maesteg, also in Bridgend county, to Australia in the 1950s.

Despite these strong roots in the country, she told Adams she was rarely able to visit, so jumped at the chance.

The Parkgate Hotel was another location for filming in June

The filmmaker likened the project to a small football team going on a cup run, saying it "brought people together in the story".

He explained: "They're still talking about it down my local pub.

"It's like there's still people that would stop me and kind of want to talk about their favourite Tarantino film or Kylie's records.

"I'm sure one day, I'll have time to sit down and actually think about it all properly.

"At the moment, it just feels like this beautiful haze that is the heart of this film."

Adams says people will continue to talk about the movie in Porthcawl for a long time

Adams said it felt right to do most of the filming in Wales' capital Cardiff and his hometown for what was such a personal movie.

He also loved the process of showing what his star cast was capable of but not necessarily known for.

Tarantino is better known for his work behind the camera, while Minogue has become one of the world's most famous pop stars after leaving Australian soap Neighbours in the late 1980s.

Adams also liked the fact his improv approach gave them freedom over their characters in a way that might not be possible on other productions.

While there is no current release date, the director is aiming for summer 2027.

He also hopes Cardiff can play host to a premiere, with his star cast attending.

"I think you've got to be very grateful that you were able to work with them," he added.

"It was about bringing a spirit a joy to south Wales."

MN202611_1fcozs9hw93.t:
'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shift

Two business owners, half a country apart, want the same thing for different reasons.

In Texas, Kim Hanks, who owns Tillies, a hotel, restaurant and spa business near Austin, says rising grocery and fuel costs are forcing her to raise wages for her 300 staff.

"It's been such a moving target for us on affordability," she told the BBC World Service.

In Indiana, Danny Reynolds, who runs Stephenson's of Elkhart, a clothing and bridalwear store, simply wants Washington to get its act together.

"My hope is that we can just find some consistency, some working together," he said.

"We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability," said House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on MS Now's Morning Joe.

But here comes the difficult part. Democrats will hold Congress. Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans.

House Democrat leader Hakeem Jeffries said "now it's our job to govern on affordability"

The scale of the win was bigger than most forecasters expected, with at least seven Republican-held Senate seats changing hands.

Behind the result was a striking mood: just 21% of Americans are satisfied with the direction of the country, even though the economy looks healthy on paper.

Voters weren't looking at the statistics. They were looking at their grocery bills, electricity bills and the price at the petrol pump.

In rural Texas, rising costs were even hurting Republicans in their own backyard. Sid Miller, the outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner, told me ranchers are getting $300 to $500 less for each head of cattle, while also facing record fertiliser costs.

This was more than a blue wave. It was a vote about the cost of living. So what can Democrats actually do about it?

The outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner for Texas Sid Miller says ranchers 'feel betrayed'

Under the banner "Fighting for an Affordable America," Democrats say healthcare is their first priority.

They want to bring back the extra financial help that made health insurance cheaper under the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid signed by President Trump in 2025.

Next come tariffs and energy. Democrats want to scrap the president's import taxes, which they say add thousands of dollars a year to the cost of groceries, fertiliser and building materials.

They also want to end the war in Iran, which they link to petrol prices averaging $4.18 a gallon, marking an increase of nearly 40%.

Housing is next. Some Democrats want to build four million new homes over the next decade.

On tax, they want to make billionaires pay more and increase tax credits for families with children.

It's a long list. But how much of it can they actually deliver?

Investor Ken Fisher, founder of Fisher Investments, puts it bluntly:

"Congress can't get anything past a presidential veto. President Trump can't get anything he wants."

The result, he says, is likely to be two years of relative quiet on the legislative and regulatory front.

In other words, winning in Congress does not give Democrats a free hand. President Trump can still block legislation, and getting around a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.

Import taxes now account for more than 5% of federal revenue

For voters hoping for lower bills, that may be a disappointing result. They didn't vote for political deadlock.

Take tariffs. Trump is unlikely to abandon a trade policy that is central to his agenda. Democrats will need Republican support if they want to change it.

Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics, expects the average tariff rate on imports to stay around 10% for the rest of Trump's term.

Tariffs are bringing in more money for the government. Import taxes accounted for just over 1% of federal revenue in 2024. This year, they account for more than 5%.

That growing contribution to government income, Yaros argues, will make tariffs "tough for a future administration to fully dismantle."

What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

President Trump told CNBC he could work with Democrats on "many more things than people understand".

Yaros sees the possibility of a big political trade-off: Democrats agree to extend Republican tax cuts in return for restoring health insurance subsidies. But he doesn't expect a deal until late 2027, with the economic benefits arriving in 2028. That's a long time to wait for anyone struggling with bills today.

Oregon Democrat Ron Wyden, who is set to chair the Finance Committee, says he will seek to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy

Democrats could also turn up the pressure on businesses.

Henrietta Treyz of consultants Veda Partners says Democrats will question companies that passed on the cost of tariffs to customers.

After the Supreme Court ruling in February, she says, the question will be: "Did you turn around, take that tariff rebate, and then lower prices for consumers?"

Companies will also be asked: "What did you get in exchange?"

Democrats, she adds, will "pick and choose very carefully."

In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat set to chair the Finance Committee, has summed up his approach in six words: "affordability for us, accountability for them."

He says he will use the committee to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy. Insurers, drugmakers and banks should expect to be called to explain themselves.

And some of the biggest changes may happen closer to home. State governors and regulators have a say in electricity prices, while local authorities decide where new homes can be built.

Democrats have won governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where the rising cost of electricity for data centres is already a concern.

The hardest test may be something Democrats cannot fix with a new law.

The price of petrol, diesel and fertiliser will depend heavily on what happens in the war with Iran. And forecasters disagree about what comes next.

Oxford Economics warns that with the election over, further escalation "appears more likely," because petrol prices will no longer be as much of a political concern for the president.

And here's the awkward part. If prices come down, Democrats may struggle to claim the credit. If they go up, they may share the blame.

There is an immediate test, too. Government funding runs out after 11 December, and the chances of another shutdown look uncomfortably high.

Democrats won the argument. Now they have to show they can make life cheaper.

You can listen to an in-depth discussion about all these issues on a special edition of Business Daily's Power Players out soon.

The pound has risen to its highest overall level since the Brexit referendum over a decade ago.

Sterling has risen notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected rise in interest rates.

The most-watched measure of the value of the British currency against a basket of 18 of the world's main currencies this week reached its joint highest level since the June 2016 referendum, according to Bank of England figures.

The value reached 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank will officially confirm the calculation on Thursday.

The value of sterling fell significantly after the Brexit referendum in June 2016, and reached further lows during the Brexit process, the Covid pandemic and the 2022 mini-Budget.

Some traders said the UK was being seen in a different light given relative political stability, solid growth and the rapprochement with the European Union.

Sterling has responded strongly to Brexit developments and political uncertainty in recent years.

Jim O'Neill, an economist and former Treasury minister, said: "I'm not surprised. People were, and to a lesser extent, are, underestimating the improving momentum in the UK."

A stronger pound can help rein in inflation, and increase buying power for consumers on imports and on holidays.

UK growth so far this year has outperformed all forecasts, but there are signs that higher energy and fuel prices have now hit consumer confidence.

The Bank's nine-member Monetary Policy Committee faces an important decision on interest rates on Thursday, with the first rise in three years widely expected .

The pound was up 0.13% against the dollar at $1.3495 and 0.16% lower against the euro at €1.1979 as of 04:15 GMT on Thursday.

With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?

Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.

In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election .

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate .

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.

But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?

Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.

BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad

THE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key results

ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now

'A DISASTER': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."

Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.

That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.

Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.

The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.

Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.

It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.

Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).

Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.

Andy Burnham has ruled out reparations but is open to a formal apology

The UK has signed up to "structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith" talks that address the "historical harms" of the transatlantic slave trade, Commonwealth leaders in Antigua have said.

The formal conclusions marking the end of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as the communique, is the joint text setting out what has been agreed.

The 18 page document , external includes a paragraph in which the leaders "welcome the agreement of the Government of the United Kingdom to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms".

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology on behalf of the UK for its role in the slave trade, while ruling out the prospect of reparations.

Officials said the timeframe for the talks would be agreed at a later date, though the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested they are likely to conclude in around a year.

Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders' summit in Manchester next November, Miliband told BBC Newscast , external : "Broadly speaking, yes."

The communique was signed after the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda

The rationale among British diplomats in committing to the wording in the communique is to try to offer reassurance that there is a sense of urgency to deal with the issue, even if a date for doing so is not yet confirmed.

This will be determined, sources said, in the "structured dialogue" the UK is promising with countries that have long demanded that the pain and lasting legacies of the slave trade are, as they see it, properly addressed.

Burnham said his "new approach with the Commonwealth" had been "well received" at the summit.

He said it had "been the most successful meeting of the Commonwealth in recent times," adding that "the King's words have resonated powerfully here and we're really pleased with how it's gone".

King Charles III, speaking in his role as Head of the Commonwealth, told the meeting: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other Members of our Commonwealth.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

MN202611_13xetk47q0y.t:
Australia's oldest department store, David Jones, has gone into voluntary administration

David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.

It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.

David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.

"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".

Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".

David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.

Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.

"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.

By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.

For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.

But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.

"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."

Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.

"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.

"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired – they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.

During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

MN202611_8pgel09b1u.t:
Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's condition

If you could find out if you had a gene that would cut your life short, would you?

This is the dilemma Laura Sides faced when she was offered a test for the rare form of early onset dementia that her dad was diagnosed with in his 40s.

Laura spoke to Dr Sian Williams, host of BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, about her decision to take the test and how it has shaped the rest of her life.

Growing up, Laura says she always felt close to her dad as they had a "similar nature". He was a GP and "the most amazing doting father," she says. When his Alzheimer's symptoms became more severe, Laura dropped out of university to care for him.

"We did have a really lovely time," she says, remembering trips to a lighthouse and collecting coasters. " I'd run him baths and just play music and pour jugs of hot water over his head and he loved it."

Laura had just celebrated her 21st birthday when she began caring for her dad

It was at a hospital appointment with her dad when a doctor told Laura she had a 50/50 chance of developing the same type of early onset Alzheimer's known as the "London variant".

"All I could think was, that's a toss of a coin," she says. "I was still so involved with what was going on with him [her dad]. I just pushed it really, really deep down."

Laura's dad died in 2009, just a year after her mum had died.

"All of a sudden I got such an overwhelming urge to leave," she says. So she booked a solo around-the-world trip, eventually settling in Melbourne, Australia.

It was there that thoughts of inheriting her dad's condition "started creeping in" and she went to see a specialist in 2013.

He told her a test could determine with 99.999% certainty if she would inherit early onset dementia. If she had the gene, her expected age of decline would be 46 to 48, he said.

"I just thought, I'm not there yet. I don't want to do that."

'Toss of a coin’ if I’d inherit dementia gene

As Laura entered her 30s she found herself thinking about the test more and more and decided she wanted to know. But first, she had to undergo six months of genetic counselling.

"There's not many realms in life where you find out your fate and it can be very difficult information to process," she says.

After a six-week wait for the test results to come through, the day finally arrived. Laura says she felt "extremely nervous".

She had booked a table for lunch with a friend afterwards - but went into the appointment alone.

"I said, 'Let's cut straight to it.' They said, 'We're really sorry, it's not good news, and you have inherited the gene.'"

She remembers "almost a white blurry noise of just sitting there".

"I came out of that room and my friend burst into hysterical tears." But Laura didn't react. "We went for our lunch and it was lovely. I don't know if it'd sunk in."

The reality hit later. "I was angry. I felt it was so unjust. I was just too confused at how I was meant to live now. How do you live with that knowledge?"

Laura has taken part in medical trials all over the world

Laura began to feel a pull back home to the UK, especially as her sister was pregnant. "It doesn't make sense... to live on the other side of the world when she's going to have a baby."

However, her around-the-world travels continued as she took part in medical trials before and after her diagnosis.

"It felt like such a positive to be involved in something out of such a negative situation."

Laura (right) is a chef and owns a cafe restaurant and catering business with two friends

Laura is now 43 - three years away from the age doctors predicted she will begin to notice symptoms.

"I keep waiting for something to sort of hit home. I guess one day I'll start declining but that doesn't keep me up at night."

She is "grateful and so lucky for the people in her life". But meeting anyone new is hard.

"Do I tell them? Do I not tell them? At what point do I tell them?

"And more often than not, when I have told them, it ends."

However she says she has been "proven wrong".

"I have been shown I can be loved despite this. It fills my heart with reassurance and joy".

Laura says she had always "naively assumed" she would be a mother.

"[Its] one of the very few things that I never questioned that I'd be good at and I wanted to do. That's hard... but it doesn't make sense to do it. It wouldn't be fair."

Laura loves swimming and is aiming to swim in as many seas as possible

For Laura, life is now about tapping in to things that "make her happy".

"It's not about huge aspirations. It's not like I want to see the Grand Canyon... I want to have time now around the people that I adore and make me feel safe.

"I love nature. I love being outside. I'm obsessed with being submerged in water. It sounds so corny, but...I believe it really is actually the little things are the big things.

"I hope I just have a wonderful few years in this world... drinking champagne and eating oysters - two of my favourite things."

Like many neighbouring countries, Guinea-Bissau waits until babies are six weeks old to vaccinate them against hepatitis B, while the WHO says it should be done at birth (file photo)

A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".

The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.

Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.

The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.

Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.

The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.

The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.

It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot .

Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.

Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.

Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.

But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.

The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025 .

Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.

He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.

"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."

He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.

Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.

Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.

The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.

"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.

Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.

Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.

Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.

"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."

The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.

Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.

"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.

His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.

SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.

The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.

Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.

He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.

Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.

He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.

On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.

Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.

They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.

The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.

Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.

The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.

Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.

Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.

Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.

There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.

MN202611_g2eklq7h2k.t:
The NHS is relying more on charities - and that might be creating problems for patients

The distress of the man on the other end of the video call was clear to dementia specialist nurse Louise Burns. He was struggling to get his elderly mum, who had the condition, out of hospital - she needed support to move into her home.

Burns was able to put him at ease. She is part of a team running virtual clinics that support more than 100 patients and family members a week: "No matter what stage they are at, we try to help," she says. She explained the discharge process and where to go for help. The man's mother was soon back where she wanted to be.

Traditionally, a service like this would have been run by the National Health Service – but the clinic, which was set up during Covid and continued because of strong demand, is entirely funded by the charity Dementia UK.

The charity's chief nursing officer Paul Edwards says it is "trying to fill the gaps" within stretched NHS services. Burns adds: "The NHS and social care are under such huge pressure and dementia cases are rising - it's not always easy to get the support you need."

Dementia UK is just one of many charities working in the health sphere. From children's care to mental health and cancer services, charities are playing an increasingly important role in caring for patients.

In her clinic, Louise Burns (left) helps patients who may be struggling with a recent diagnosis or who have noticed worrying symptoms

Some - largely in England - have formal NHS contracts, while others work side-by-side with the health service across the UK, trying to provide additional support to patients in a way the NHS cannot.

A desire from governments of different parties from the 1990s onwards to develop a market of providers – NHS, private and voluntary sector – has meant the charity sector is now big business in health.

It's estimated that cancer charities alone raise more than £1bn a year, and the NHS in England spends nearly £2bn a year buying services from the not-for-profit and voluntary sector.

But there are concerns about the scale of charities' involvement in delivering frontline services - including from within the voluntary sector itself. Those directly providing services say they are having to subsidise squeezed NHS budgets.

And despite the good intentions of the charitable sector, some critics say its work with the NHS means more money ends up in wealthier communities. Defenders of charities' involvement, however, say much-needed funding should be welcomed.

So is the growing role of charities a symptom of a health service at breaking point - or a positive way of involving the public in their health care? And what are the risks?

There's nothing new about UK health charities taking on a major role in delivering services. Prior to 1948, British healthcare was provided through a patchwork of local charities, voluntary organisations, local authorities and private arrangements. Many hospitals depended on charitable donations, subscriptions and fundraising events to survive.

The creation of the NHS transformed this model. Most hospitals were brought into public ownership and funded through taxation. NHS founder Aneurin Bevan believed healthcare should not depend on charity, and restrictions were placed on NHS hospital charities actively raising money. But they did not disappear completely - they could still receive gifts and donations.

A major shift came with the Health Services Act 1980, which encouraged a more active fundraising culture. From then on, NHS charities expanded significantly and became increasingly professionalised. By the 1990s and beyond, they were raising substantial sums for equipment, buildings, research, and the likes of play areas in children's wards and well-equipped staff rooms.

Today, distinct from charities devoted to particular diseases or conditions, there are now more than 220 NHS charities attached to hospitals or community services, which raise £620m a year.

Ellie Orton, chief executive of NHS Charities Together, which represents them, says that while this sum may sound high, it represents only around 0.3% of the health budget.

She says the very purpose of the charities is to provide support, equipment and services that are additional to what the NHS provides. Recent schemes involve things like CPR training for members of the public, defibrillators being placed in community venues and green spaces in hospitals.

But it is a fine line. Scanners, blood transfusion equipment and emergency department co-ordinators have also been funded by charities. Some would say say core NHS functions like these are exactly what we pay our taxes for.

Orton defends this. "It's just the way it is now. We shouldn't get too ideological about this. It's not helpful to think the state can do everything. Yes we pay taxes but that has to cover lots – and it's finite. If our fund-raising means a parent of an ill child can stay close to their child while they are in hospital in a room funded by a charity, why not?"

Sir Kevin Sinfield (right) has helped raise millions for motor neurone disease patients

And she says her discussions with the government suggest that there is increasing interest in what charities can raise and also what larger philanthropic donations by individuals or organisations can achieve.

In recent years, huge one-off sums have been raised. During the pandemic, the NHS Charities Together Covid appeal resulted in a £10m donation by the trading firm XTX Markets, while the Rausing family - best known for founding the food packaging giant Tetra Pak – gave £5m.

Rugby league legend Sir Kevin Sinfield's fundraising in support of his friend Rob Burrow helped bring in £6.8m for a specialist motor neurone disease centre at Leeds Teaching Hospitals.

"Of course, we are not talking about going back to a pre-1948 situation, but there is real interest in what such philanthropy can do," says Orton.

But there are inequalities. The NHS charity sector is dominated by some of the big London hospitals and specialist cancer and children's centres. The Royal Marsden and Great Ormond Street charities between them are responsible for nearly a sixth of the investment made by NHS charities.

"This does concern us," admits Orton. "It's not always a level playing field, but the answer to that is to help the NHS charities that don't raise as much to raise more."

The legislation change in the 1980s, coupled with the market reforms of the 1990s, also helped pave the way for specialist disease-specific charities such as Macmillan, Marie Curie and Dementia UK to get involved in the delivery of NHS services.

For example, over the past three decades, Dementia UK has developed a well-established network of specialist dementia nurses known as Admiral Nurses, who work in a range of hospital and community settings. The model is based on the charity co-funding posts with the NHS for up to two years with the expectation that the NHS will then take on the funding.

But with demand increasing, Edwards says it is becoming a "struggle" to get the funding needed from the NHS or from donations. "We are being asked to fund them for longer or find more than half the cost," he says. "Services are really being cut back."

And it is not just in dementia care that charities are noticing a squeeze. The charity WellChild has helped establish a network of 54 specialist nurses who work with very sick children. It funds these posts for the first three years, before responsibility for funding is expected to transfer to the NHS.

But disappointingly for the charity, for the first time this year a nurse post was not kept on, says Amy Mitchell, WellChild's director of programmes. What's more, WellChild's nurses are only meant to carry a caseloads of 15, but the average is currently 40. "Services are being dismantled - and our nurses are propping things up," Mitchell adds.

Others in the voluntary sector agree. Charities are increasingly being asked to do more with less, says Mark Yates, chief operating officer of Rethink Mental Illness, "and there is too often an expectation that we will absorb shortfalls ourselves to keep essential services running".

Parkinson's UK told the BBC its funding has helped the NHS pay for around 70% of the specialist nurses working in the field - and its chief executive officer Caroline Rassell says it's unfair on people affected by the disease.

"Charities having to fund these posts is effectively an additional 'tax' on people with Parkinson's as they are our main donors," says Rassell. "Nursing care should be the cornerstone of what the NHS offers."

Polling by the National Council for Voluntary Organisations shows 71% of health charities say the value of their contracts are not enough to meet the demand for the services they provide with many using their own donations to keep them going.

The survey dates back to 2023, but the NCVO says there is nothing to suggest the situation has eased.

NCVO chief influencing officer Leigh Brimicombe says it's quite clear charities are having to "subsidise" the NHS and wider public services and the government needs to address it by offering contracts that "cover the full cost of delivery".

"Otherwise, we run the risk of services being reduced or cut completely, at a time that communities in need are relying on them most."

For its part, the NHS is adamant that charities remain a valuable partner. NHS England points out that while the value of contracts to the voluntary sector in terms of proportion of the budget has dropped, it has still risen in cash terms.

In a statement, NHS England told the BBC the current 10-year plan looks to build on the "potential" of these partnerships and given the sector a "stronger voice" in health and care.

It's a complex relationship, believes Helen Gilburt, of the King's Fund think tank. Charities bring "real benefits" through their expertise and close ties to communities, she says, and there is "an element of subsidising" as the NHS seeks savings. But the situation has also "created inequalities" in the funding and support available for different diseases, she believes.

For instance, some areas, like cancer, have an established charitable sector "which is able to attract large amounts of funding", she says. These charities have been able to advocate for their patients, work with the NHS to enhance specialist services, and use their funds to develop services of their own.

Then, she says, there are charities in some sectors - "Parkinson's and dementia are good examples" – which are investing their own funds to develop specialist roles. "But they would argue this does not go far enough to meet the needs of people they serve.

"Then there are other areas, like sickle cell disease for example, where the charity sector is small and has even less funding."

Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?

A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science

Inequalities exist within sectors, too, say experts. Take hospices, for instance. "The fact remains that some communities will be able to give more than others, leading to inequalities in hospice provision," says Toby Porter, chief executive officer of Hospice UK.

And as a result, says Sarah Scobie, deputy director of research at the Nuffield Trust think tank, "more people from deprived areas die in the place where most people say they don't want to die – in hospital".

Not all of these differences can be explained by fundraising capacity. Health literacy – people's ability to navigate services and advocate for themselves – can also affect access to support, she says.

But her concern is clear – the scale of charity involvement in the NHS can widen inequalities.

As Orton points out, the UK is not returning to the pre-NHS era, when healthcare depended on charitable giving. Yet charities are no longer operating on the margins of the system, either.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub , the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility ( word error rate of the outputs ), speed ( inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio ), and naturalness ( UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean ). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish , and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts , specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile , e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer , held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices .

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio . Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.
